title: Virtual Biotech: trace the claim from association to proposed intervention
author: Codex conversation; exact model identifier not recorded
workflow: MAR skill evidence challenge and synthesis
summary: This review covers the February 2026 preprint. It identifies three revision priorities, two verification questions, one supported strength and five dismissed concerns. The assessments distinguish the reported computational results from mechanistic, treatment-selection and comparative-quality conclusions.
coverage: Read: abstract, main text, Extended Methods, five figure captions and data availability in the 23 February 2026 preprint v1 (PMC12970349.1). The offline CLI produced 30 leads from 150 source blocks. One model-native synthesis followed the MAR evidence-challenge checklist; no provider panel or independent expert assessment was run. Supplementary PDF, figure images, execution logs, source code and raw datasets were not inspected. The September 2026 Science version is outside this review.

items.title: B7-H3 association and mechanism
items.assessment: The reported evidence links B7-H3 expression with spatial cell patterns and survival. These observational associations do not establish that changing B7-H3 activity causes or reverses immune exclusion. Describing them as “functional evidence” needs qualification.
items.challenge: The methods exclude B7-H3 from cell-abundance estimation and account for spatial composition and sample effects. The discussion also identifies the case studies as hypotheses requiring validation.
items.next_step: Revise the mechanistic wording to reflect observational evidence. If a causal claim is required, propose a new study perturbing B7-H3 in matched fibroblast, immune-cell and tumor systems across independent donors. Compare appropriate controls and measure immune exclusion or function, with viability checks.
items.decision_change: Replicated interventions separating B7-H3 activity from correlated fibroblast state would support stronger mechanistic language.

items.title: OSMR expression and treatment selection
items.assessment: Baseline oncostatin M receptor (OSMR) expression is associated with nonresponse to other biologics. This does not establish greater benefit from vixarelimab in a selected subgroup or explain why MOONGLOW stopped.
items.challenge: The authors use conditional language, describe the case studies as hypotheses and identify unresolved assay and cutoff choices. The review should retain those qualifications.
items.next_step: Check whether baseline biopsies, randomized treatment assignments and outcomes from MOONGLOW are available. If available, estimate whether treatment effects vary with the biomarker, including uncertainty. An exploratory result would require a prespecified assay and cutoff plus independent prospective evaluation before supporting a validated selection strategy.
items.decision_change: Treatment-interaction evidence replicated in an independent cohort could justify predictive language. General association with disease severity or other-therapy nonresponse would not.

items.title: Dependence across trials
items.assessment: Related trials can share drugs, targets and molecular features. The reported modality and disease-area random effects do not establish that this dependence is accounted for, and shuffling individual outcomes may not preserve it. The effect on uncertainty remains unverified.
items.challenge: The paper reports adjusted mixed models, adjustment for genetic evidence, correction for multiple comparisons and an observational limitation. These address other sources of bias and uncertainty.
items.next_step: Inspect the trial–drug–target mapping and scripts; count independent groups and their overlap. If dependence remains, compare uncertainty using a variance model or resampling scheme that accounts for shared drugs, programs or targets, including drugs with multiple targets. Claims about future prediction also need evaluation on later trials and unseen groups. The required mapping and code were not audited.
items.decision_change: Existing adequate dependence handling in code, or stable effect sizes and uncertainty under the appropriate grouped analysis, would close or narrow this concern.

items.title: Evidence for comparative review quality
items.assessment: The case studies, API expenditure and parallel execution demonstrate feasibility. They do not measure improvement over human teams or the contribution of the reviewer agent to scientific accuracy. API expenditure also does not measure total project cost.
items.challenge: The authors describe an inspectable workflow and acknowledge that agent errors can propagate. These observations do not substitute for a controlled comparison.
items.next_step: Qualify comparative claims. A validation study could compare the full workflow, a version without the reviewer and a simpler agent on the same unseen questions, information and budget. Blinded experts would assess correct conclusions, unsupported claims and missing evidence; record time and total cost. This study was not performed for the showcase.
items.decision_change: A controlled assessment showing repeatable quality gains would support a stronger claim about the reviewer loop. Reported case costs alone would not.

items.title: Reviewer feedback leads to a follow-up analysis
items.assessment: The reviewer identifies missing spatial context, and the workflow follows with a spatial analysis. This documents a specific link between a criticism and an analysis addressing it.
items.challenge: The case studies remain observational hypotheses requiring validation. The example does not measure improvement in review accuracy.
items.next_step: Retain this example as a rationale for linking each MAR concern to a specific next check. Evaluate its effect on review quality in a future blinded comparison.
items.decision_change: If logs showed that the follow-up was unrelated to the critique, the claimed workflow example would weaken; execution logs were not audited.

items.title: Donor and sample effects are reported
items.assessment: The methods aggregate counts by donor and cell type and include patient effects for longitudinal ulcerative colitis data. The generic contradiction combines different analyses; the evidence does not support a blanket concern about absent donor control.
items.challenge: A sample intercept is also reported for spatial data. Trial reuse and correlation within a slide remain distinct questions.
items.next_step: Close the generic contradiction. Inspect a specific model and its independent biological unit before raising a dependence concern.
items.decision_change: A mismatch between the described and executed analysis could justify a specific issue.

items.title: “First trained” describes analysis order
items.assessment: The engine matched “first” in a methods description of model fitting. It refers to the order of analysis steps, not a claim of scientific priority.
items.challenge: The surrounding paragraph describes reference fitting followed by spatial mapping; there is no novelty assertion in this evidence span.
items.next_step: Discard this particular novelty lead. Any actual priority or originality claim needs a separate literature check.
items.decision_change: A different passage making an explicit first-ever claim would need its own evidence and review.

items.title: Reported thresholds and endpoints
items.assessment: The paper reports a cell-type specificity (tau) threshold and spatial quartiles within samples. Endpoint failures and successes refer to different trials. The proposed OSMR enrollment cutoff is a separate, unresolved choice.
items.challenge: A reported threshold does not establish robustness to its choice. Trials with multiple treatment groups may also require further annotation checks.
items.next_step: Close the generic missing-cutoff and contradictory-endpoint leads. Tie any sensitivity or annotation question to the analysis it could affect.
items.decision_change: An inconsistent definition for the same outcome or an unreported threshold used in a main analysis would reopen a specific reporting concern.

items.title: Reproducibility and annotation uncertainty
items.assessment: The paper describes downloadable code and reports, plus human annotation checks. This review did not execute a pinned release or inspect the full supplementary protocol. Agreement on the checked subset does not establish accuracy across all annotations or quantify the effect of remaining errors.
items.challenge: The article reports two human annotators and a comparison with the Therapeutic Data Commons (TDC) dataset. Human validation is present; its coverage and the effect of annotation errors require assessment.
items.next_step: Locate the exact code and data release and supplementary annotation rules. Check missing data, disagreement patterns, random seeds, assay and threshold sensitivity, and tool versions. Test whether plausible annotation errors change key results. Treat uninspected details as open checks.
items.decision_change: A reproducible release plus an adequate error/missingness sensitivity analysis could close these checks. A confirmed execution or annotation failure would justify a narrower issue.

items.title: Original-screen checks do not apply to reused data
items.assessment: The workflow reuses Tahoe perturbation profiles. This does not establish that the study performed a new pooled screen, so screen-specific control requirements cannot be inferred from those terms alone.
items.challenge: Dataset provenance and the validity of the reused signatures remain relevant, but must be checked against the original data and the actual analysis.
items.next_step: Mark original-screen reporting leads out of scope; route provenance checks to the source dataset and released analysis.
items.decision_change: If a new original screen were supplied, the corresponding experimental controls would become applicable.

items.title: Batch handling is described
items.assessment: The manuscript describes Harmony preprocessing. This answers the generic reporting concern about absent batch handling; whether the correction is adequate requires the data and study design.
items.challenge: The authors acknowledge residual confounding in the observational trial analysis. Naming a correction method does not establish that all relevant confounding is removed.
items.next_step: Close the reporting-absence lead. Assess any remaining confounding against a specific comparison and conclusion.
items.decision_change: Evidence that a relevant cohort/platform effect is inseparable from the biological contrast would justify a focused concern.

assessment.text: The preprint reports computational case studies and observational associations. These generate therapeutic hypotheses; causal mechanisms and treatment-specific benefit remain untested. Trial-level uncertainty requires verification.

contribution.text: Documents a reviewer critique followed by a spatial analysis addressing the missing tissue context.

priorities.text: Describe B7-H3 findings as spatial and survival associations. A causal mechanism requires intervention evidence.
Keep enrollment based on oncostatin M receptor (OSMR) expression as a hypothesis: nonresponse to other therapies does not establish benefit from vixarelimab.
Check whether uncertainty accounts for drugs, targets and development programs represented in multiple trials.

first_step.text: Align the claims with the observational evidence, then inspect the trial–drug–target mapping to assess dependence.

at_a_glance.scope: February 2026 preprint v1, not the later journal article. Offline CLI plus model-native synthesis; text, methods and captions reviewed. Supplements, code and data were not inspected; no independent human validation of this review.
